toc.title: Where Scrum Theory Shows Up in the Framework
Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1Scrum in One Sentence

"Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems."

Part of the definition What it means for the exam
Lightweight framework Few rules, not a detailed method. The framework is "purposefully incomplete, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory"
People, teams and organizations Scrum serves all three levels, which is why the Scrum Master also serves the organization (Topic 5)
Generate value The aim is value for customers and the organization, not output for its own sake
Adaptive solutions The answer is not fixed in advance: the team learns and adjusts as it goes
Complex problems Work whose results cannot be fully predicted. Scrum is built for it

1.1 The nutshell (four steps)

The Guide says Scrum requires a Scrum Master to foster an environment where:

  1. A Product Owner orders the work for a complex problem into a Product Backlog.
  2. The Scrum Team turns a selection of the work into an Increment of value during a Sprint.
  3. The Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint.
  4. Repeat.

1.2 What the Guide adds about the framework

  • Scrum is simple. "Try it as is" and decide whether its philosophy, theory and structure help to achieve goals and create value.
  • It is built upon the collective intelligence of the people using it. Rather than detailed instructions, the rules of Scrum guide relationships and interactions.
  • Other techniques fit inside it. Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework. Scrum "wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary" and makes visible how well current management, environment and work techniques work, so that they can be improved.
  • Patterns beyond the Guide are not part of Scrum. Insights and tactics that fit the framework are "context sensitive" and are described elsewhere.
Exam angle

Scrum is a framework, not a methodology or a process with step-by-step instructions. An option that says Scrum prescribes how to write requirements, estimate or test is wrong: those choices are made by the Scrum Team inside the framework.

2Scrum Theory

Scrum "is founded on empiricism and lean thinking."

Idea Guide wording Practical meaning
Empiricism (SF 1.3) Knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed Decide from real results (the Increment, the Sprint outcome), not from guesses made at the start
Lean thinking Reduces waste and focuses on the essentials Work on what matters most, and stop doing what adds no value

Two more statements from the Guide's theory section:

  • Scrum uses an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and to control risk (section 4 below).
  • Scrum engages groups of people who collectively have all the skills and expertise to do the work and share or acquire such skills as needed (Topic 3).

Scrum combines four formal events for inspection and adaptation within a containing event, the Sprint. These events work "because they implement the empirical Scrum pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation."

Old wording

The 2017 Guide said Scrum is founded on "empirical process control theory, or empiricism", and that "three pillars uphold every implementation of empirical process control." It also described Scrum as "lightweight, simple to understand, difficult to master". The 2020 Guide uses empiricism and lean thinking and does not use "difficult to master". Lean thinking is new in 2020.

3The Three Pillars (SF 1.4)

Pillar What the Guide says What goes wrong without it
Transparency The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving it. Important decisions are based on the perceived state of the three formal artifacts Low transparency "can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk". Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful
Inspection The artifacts and the progress toward agreed goals are inspected frequently and diligently to detect potentially undesirable variances or problems. The five events give the cadence Inspection without adaptation is pointless. Events are "designed to provoke change"
Adaptation If any aspect of a process deviates outside acceptable limits, or the product is unacceptable, the process or the materials must be adjusted as soon as possible to minimize further deviation Adaptation is harder when people are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team adapts "the moment it learns anything new through inspection"

The pillars depend on one another in a chain: transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation. The Scrum values (Topic 2) are what make the pillars "come to life, building trust."

Exam angle

the pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. Courage, openness, focus, commitment and respect are values, not pillars. Questions often swap the two lists.

4Iterative and Incremental (SF 1.5)

The Guide says Scrum "employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and to control risk." It names the Sprint as the unit of that approach: Sprints are the heartbeat of Scrum, each is "a short project", and every Increment is additive to all prior Increments.

Term Meaning Where it shows in Scrum
Iterative Work in repeated cycles, using what was learned in one cycle to improve the next Each Sprint inspects and adapts; the Product Backlog is reordered after each Review
Incremental Build the product in usable slices, each adding to the previous ones Each Increment is usable and added to all prior Increments

4.1 Benefits (list at least three) Beyond the Guide

The Guide states two aims (predictability, control of risk). The other benefits are the usual ones taught for the learning objective.

Benefit Why
Earlier and more frequent feedback Stakeholders inspect a real Increment at every Sprint Review, not a plan
Earlier delivery of value Usable Increments exist from the first Sprints; the Review "should never be considered a gate to releasing value"
Lower risk Each Sprint limits cost and effort to a short time frame; "shorter Sprints can be employed to generate more learning cycles and limit risk"
Better predictability The team inspects and adapts progress toward the Product Goal at least every calendar month
Ability to respond to change The Product Backlog is emergent, so new information can change the order of the work
Continuous learning and improvement Every Retrospective feeds improvements into the next Sprint
Exam angle

if an option lists a benefit of iterative and incremental work, choose the one about feedback, risk, value or adaptability. Options that promise "no changes after planning", "less need to talk to stakeholders" or "a fixed scope at the start" are the opposite of Scrum.

5Complex Work and Empiricism

The Guide places Scrum in complex work: "In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making."

  • Practices to forecast progress, such as burn-downs, burn-ups or cumulative flows, are "proven useful", but "do not replace the importance of empiricism."
  • A long Sprint is a risk: when a Sprint's horizon is too long, the Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise and risk may increase (Topic 6).
  • Scrum has spread beyond software. The Guide uses the word "developers" for everyone who does the work: "not to exclude, but to simplify. If you get value from Scrum, consider yourself included."
Detailed up-front prediction Empiricism
Plan everything first, then follow the plan Plan a little, learn from results, plan again
Changes are exceptions to control New information is expected and used
Progress is judged against the plan Progress is judged by the inspected Increment
Risk is addressed at the start Risk is limited in every short cycle

6Scrum Is Immutable: Partial Scrum (SF 1.6)

The Guide's End Note: "Scrum is free and offered in this Guide. The Scrum framework, as outlined herein, is immutable. While implementing only parts of Scrum is possible, the result is not Scrum. Scrum exists only in its entirety and functions well as a container for other techniques, methodologies, and practices."

The opening of the Guide gives the reason. First, "each element of the framework serves a specific purpose that is essential to the overall value and results realized with Scrum". Then: "Changing the core design or ideas of Scrum, leaving out elements, or not following the rules of Scrum, covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless."

6.1 Disadvantages of partial Scrum (at least two) Beyond the Guide

If an element is left out What is lost
Sprint Retrospective The only event dedicated to improving how the team works: the same problems repeat
Definition of Done Transparency of the Increment: nobody knows what "done" means, and quality drifts
Sprint Review Inspection by stakeholders: feedback arrives late and the Product Backlog is not adjusted
A single, empowered Product Owner Clear priorities and decisions: work is ordered by whoever shouts loudest
Fixed-length Sprints A regular cadence of inspection and adaptation: predictability falls and risk rises
The Scrum Master's role Help in understanding Scrum and removing impediments: Scrum erodes into old habits

General consequences: problems stay hidden (the Guide's own reason), the benefits of the empirical loop are lost, and a team can call itself "Scrum" while getting none of Scrum's results.

Exam angle

"We do Scrum, but we skip the Retrospective / have no Product Owner / extend Sprints when we are late" is not Scrum. The best answer restores the missing element and helps people see what it protects. It does not endorse the shortcut. The same Guide also says Scrum can contain other techniques: adding practices inside the framework is fine; removing parts of it is not.

7Where Scrum Theory Shows Up in the Framework

Theory element Where you see it
Transparency Three artifacts, each with a commitment (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done); the Daily Scrum; the Sprint Review
Inspection Every event is a "formal opportunity to inspect and adapt"; the Sprint Review inspects the Increment; the Retrospective inspects the way of working
Adaptation The Product Backlog is reordered; the Sprint Backlog is updated daily; the Retrospective's improvements go into the next Sprint
Lean thinking An ordered Product Backlog (essentials first); Sprint Goal focus; quality built in through the Definition of Done
Iterative and incremental Fixed-length Sprints that each produce an Increment

8Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. Pillars versus values. Pillars: transparency, inspection, adaptation. Values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage.
  2. Scrum is a framework, "purposefully incomplete". Anything about how to estimate, write requirements or test belongs to the team, not to Scrum.
  3. Empiricism means decisions based on observation and experience. Options based on early detailed prediction are wrong.
  4. Inspection without adaptation is pointless, and inspection without transparency is misleading. Look for the answer that keeps the chain intact.
  5. Adapt as soon as possible. Waiting for the end of the project, or for the next phase, contradicts the Guide.
  6. Partial Scrum is not Scrum. Dropping an event, artifact or accountability is wrong, and the answer should restore it.
  7. Scrum is not only for software. The Guide applies it to complex work in many domains.
  8. Five events, three artifacts, three commitments, three accountabilities, three pillars, five values: keep the numbers apart.
  9. Old wording "Empirical process control theory", "difficult to master" and "potentially releasable" are 2017 phrases. Answer from the 2020 wording: empiricism and lean thinking, a usable Increment.
  10. Forecasting tools (burn-down, burn-up, cumulative flow) are useful but never replace inspection of the Increment.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A new manager asks why the Scrum Team cannot simply plan the whole year in detail and then follow the plan. Which explanation of Scrum is best?

  • AScrum rests on empiricism: in complex work decisions are based on observation, so the team plans, inspects the result and adapts
  • BScrum assumes the work is simple and predictable, which is why a detailed plan followed to the letter is the safest approach
  • CScrum does allow a year-long plan, but the Scrum Master must approve it in detail before the first Sprint can start
  • DScrum applies only to the first Sprint of a product, after which a conventional detailed project plan takes over
Show the answer

Answer: A. Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking: knowledge comes from experience and decisions are based on what is observed. In complex environments what will happen is unknown, and only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decisions. The other options contradict either the theory or the framework's scope.

S2At the end of each Sprint the team demonstrates progress, but nobody ever changes the Product Backlog or the way the team works afterwards. Which pillar is missing?

  • AAdaptation, because inspection without adaptation is pointless
  • BTransparency, because the work is hidden from the stakeholders
  • CCourage, because pillars are the Scrum values
  • DInspection, because the team never looks at its work
Show the answer

Answer: A. The team inspects, but it does not adjust what it learns. The Guide says inspection without adaptation is considered pointless and that Scrum events are designed to provoke change. Transparency is present (the work is demonstrated), and courage is a value, not a pillar.

S3A team keeps its Sprints, Daily Scrums and Product Owner, but drops the Sprint Retrospective "to save time". What is the most likely effect?

  • ANo effect, because the Retrospective is not required for inspection
  • BThe same problems keep coming back, because the only event dedicated to improving how the team works is gone
  • CThe Sprint becomes longer, because the Retrospective is part of the Sprint timebox
  • DThe Product Owner loses authority over the Product Backlog
Show the answer

Answer: B. Leaving out an element of Scrum covers up problems and limits its benefits. Without the Retrospective, the team loses its planned opportunity to improve quality and effectiveness. The Retrospective does not affect the Sprint length or the Product Owner's authority.

S4A stakeholder asks why Scrum delivers an Increment in every Sprint instead of one release at the end of the project. Which answer fits the Scrum theory best?

  • ABecause Increments allow the team to avoid talking to stakeholders until the final release
  • BBecause the Guide requires every Increment to be released to customers at the end of the Sprint
  • CBecause frequent Increments make the Product Backlog unnecessary
  • DBecause a usable Increment every Sprint gives early feedback and limits risk to one short cycle
Show the answer

Answer: D. An iterative, incremental approach is used to optimize predictability and control risk. Each Sprint's Increment can be inspected, so feedback comes early and the cost of being wrong is limited. Release is a decision, not a Guide requirement, and the Product Backlog remains the single source of work.

S5A department says: "We do Scrum, but our Sprints stretch whenever the work is late." Which response best reflects the Scrum Guide?

  • AAgree, because adjusting the Sprint length to the amount of work is a normal and healthy adaptation of Scrum
  • BReport the team to the organization, because stretching Sprints is a violation that management must punish
  • CExplain that using only parts of Scrum means the result is not Scrum, and help the team see what fixed Sprints protect
  • DAsk the Product Owner to decide each time whether the Sprint may be extended, since the Product Owner is accountable for the value delivered in each Sprint
Show the answer

Answer: C. The framework is immutable: partial implementation produces something that is not Scrum. Sprints are fixed-length events that create consistency and a regular chance to inspect and adapt. The Scrum Master helps people understand the reasons rather than policing, and no one, including the Product Owner, may stretch the Sprint.

S6During a discussion, a Developer lists "courage, transparency, focus, adaptation and respect" as the five Scrum values. What should the Scrum Master point out?

  • AThe list is correct, because the Guide groups the pillars and the values together as five qualities of a Scrum Team
  • BTransparency and adaptation are pillars; the five values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage
  • CAdaptation is a value and courage is a pillar, so the list needs only that one swap to be correct
  • DThe Guide does not define either list, so any five qualities that the team finds useful may be called Scrum values
Show the answer

Answer: B. The pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. The values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. The two lists are defined separately in the Guide and are often mixed up in questions.

S7A new Scrum Team asks the Scrum Master which technique the Scrum Guide requires for sizing Product Backlog items. What is the best answer?

  • AThe Guide does not prescribe a technique: the Developers do the sizing, and the Scrum Team chooses practices that fit its work
  • BRelative story points, because Scrum requires them for sizing
  • CThe Scrum Master chooses one technique that every Scrum Team in the organization must use
  • DThe Product Owner chooses the technique, because the Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog
Show the answer

Answer: A. Scrum is a purposefully incomplete framework: it defines the parts needed to implement the theory and leaves techniques to the people using it. The Guide only says that the Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing. A required technique, whether story points or anything else, is not part of the Guide.

S8A manager says that the burn-down chart proves the project will finish on time, so the Sprint Review is no longer needed. What is the best response?

  • AAgree, because a burn-down chart is more reliable than stakeholder feedback for judging whether the project is on time
  • BAgree, but keep the Review as a short presentation for the manager alone, since the other stakeholders no longer need it
  • CAsk the Developers to replace the burn-down chart with a longer detailed plan so that the forecast can be trusted
  • DExplain that forecasts are useful but do not replace empiricism, so the Increment must still be inspected at the Review
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Guide says that burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows are proven useful but do not replace the importance of empiricism, because in a complex environment only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decisions. The Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders and is part of the framework.

S9Stakeholders say they cannot tell what the team has really finished, because many items are "almost done". Which pillar is weak, and what helps most?

  • AAdaptation, so the team should hold more planning meetings
  • BInspection, so the team should send weekly status reports
  • CTransparency, so the team should make its work visible and agree on what "Done" means
  • DCourage, so the team should work faster
Show the answer

Answer: C. Transparency means the work must be visible to those doing it and those receiving it, with a shared understanding of what has been completed. The Definition of Done gives that shared understanding. Reports and meetings do not fix a lack of shared understanding, and courage is a value, not a pillar.

9.2 Recall Q&As

R1How does the Scrum Guide define Scrum?

Show the answer

A lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems.

R2What are the four steps of Scrum "in a nutshell"?

Show the answer

A Product Owner orders the work into a Product Backlog; the Scrum Team turns a selection into an Increment during a Sprint; the Scrum Team and its stakeholders inspect the results and adjust for the next Sprint; repeat.

R3What is empiricism?

Show the answer

Knowledge comes from experience, and decisions are based on what is observed.

R4What is lean thinking?

Show the answer

Reducing waste and focusing on the essentials.

R5What are the three empirical pillars of Scrum?

Show the answer

Transparency, inspection and adaptation.

R6What does transparency enable, and what happens to inspection without it?

Show the answer

Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

R7What does the Guide say about inspection without adaptation?

Show the answer

It is considered pointless; Scrum events are designed to provoke change.

R8When must adaptation happen, and why?

Show the answer

As soon as possible, to minimize further deviation. A Scrum Team adapts the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

R9What contains the other four events?

Show the answer

The Sprint.

R10What is the difference between iterative and incremental?

Show the answer

Iterative: repeated cycles that use what was learned to improve the next. Incremental: building the product in usable slices that add to prior Increments.

R11Name at least three benefits of an iterative and incremental approach.

Show the answer

Earlier feedback, earlier delivery of value, lower risk, better predictability, ability to respond to change, continuous learning. (The Guide states predictability and risk control.)

R12What does the Guide say about implementing only parts of Scrum?

Show the answer

It is possible, but the result is not Scrum. The framework is immutable and exists only in its entirety.

R13Name at least two disadvantages of partial Scrum.

Show the answer

Problems stay hidden; benefits are lost (for example no improvement without the Retrospective, no shared quality bar without the Definition of Done, no stakeholder inspection without the Review); the team may call itself Scrum without getting Scrum's results.

R14What may be used for forward-looking decisions in a complex environment?

Show the answer

Only what has already happened. Forecasting practices do not replace empiricism.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Scrum Lightweight framework for generating value through adaptive solutions to complex problems
Nutshell Product Owner orders the Product Backlog → Scrum Team creates an Increment in a Sprint → team and stakeholders inspect and adjust → repeat
Theory Empiricism and lean thinking
Empiricism Knowledge from experience; decisions based on what is observed
Lean thinking Reduce waste; focus on essentials
Pillars Transparency → inspection → adaptation
Transparency Work visible to those doing it and those receiving it; without it inspection is misleading
Inspection Frequent and diligent; five events give the cadence; without adaptation it is pointless
Adaptation Adjust as soon as possible when things deviate or the product is unacceptable
Approach Iterative and incremental, to optimize predictability and control risk
Immutable Partial Scrum is not Scrum; Scrum is a container for other techniques
Complex work Only what has happened guides forward-looking decisions; forecasts do not replace empiricism
Old wording "Empirical process control" (2017) → empiricism and lean thinking (2020)
